title: Where should the website's COMTRAN tutorial live, and how much should it teach?
today: The public site compiles a deck in the browser and prints the 1962 compiler listing, but it cannot run the program. Draft PR #188 adds a Run button. It runs the compiled program on an emulated IBM 7090, over the two input tapes of the 1962 payroll sample. Those tapes are built into the page, under 5 KB, so a run needs no download. No tutorial text exists yet. The PR holds only an eleven-lesson outline.
why_now: The tutorial prose cannot start until its page form is fixed. You asked for a tutorial page separate from the front page, and the roadmap says that page uses the existing card editor and never a second one. Your 2 November ruling holds the comparison against the surviving 1963 compiler until this phase and the one before it are done.
if_nothing: PR #188 stays a draft, so the live site keeps no Run button and no tutorial. The comparison against the 1963 compiler stays closed behind this phase.

options.label: A separate tutorial page that reuses the front page's editor, output panels and script
options.what_changes: Each lesson sits beside the one card editor. A lesson loads a deck, and the reader presses Run on the same screen. One script means one set of card-column rules.
options.cost_risk: About 100 lines of page markup (the editor and its output panels) get copied, plus a test that keeps both copies equal. The script needs a small change to start on a second page: today it writes a build line into an element only the front page has, and fails without it.
options.reverse: Easy. Delete the page and its test.
options.example: Lesson 8 says 'change this line', the reader edits the deck, presses Run, and sees the report line move.

options.label: Put the lessons around the editor on the front page
options.what_changes: No copied markup. Eleven lessons wrap around the compiler on the first page a visitor sees.
options.cost_risk: Goes against your own request for a separate page. The front page exists to bring a reader in, and the site's copy rules cap a front-page paragraph at three sentences. Eleven lessons would bury the compiler.
options.reverse: Hard. Moving the lessons out later means rewriting the front page.

options.label: A text-only tutorial page whose examples are share links into the front page
options.what_changes: No editor code on the tutorial page. Each example is a link that opens the front page with that deck loaded. Share links already exist.
options.cost_risk: Cheapest. The reader flips between two pages and loses 'change a line, run, see the report change' on one screen. The roadmap entry 'the tutorial page, with the existing editor' would need an edit.
options.reverse: Easy, but the prose would need reworking to sit beside an editor later.

options.label: Scope alternative: a course of many small programs instead of one walk through the 1962 sample
options.what_changes: This changes what the tutorial covers, not where it lives; it combines with A, B or C. It teaches more of COMTRAN than the one payroll sample.
options.cost_risk: Any example that reads input needs its own input tapes built into the site. Each example also needs a test that keeps it compiling, or the tutorial breaks silently when the compiler changes. Writing and test cost is several times that of the walk through the sample.
options.reverse: Moderate. Examples can be added later on top of the walk.

recommendation: Take A, scoped to one guided walk through the 1962 payroll sample. It is the only form that puts the lesson and the running program on one screen with one editor, which is the roadmap's reason for refusing a second editor. Its one cost, a copied block of markup, is caught by a cheap test. Every lesson that uses the unedited sample is already pinned by the existing tests, including the warning lesson: the sample reads the retirement premium as the insurance premium, on the 1962 page and in our run, and your ruling keeps that 1962 behaviour. The lesson where the reader edits a line needs one test of its own.
prototype: Draft PR #188 adds a Run button to the site that runs the compiled program on an emulated IBM 7090 over the sample's built-in input tapes, with a seventh output panel for what it prints; all five CI checks pass. It holds the tutorial outline only, no lesson text.

scenes.heading: Where the lessons sit

options.label: A. Separate tutorial page, same editor and script
options.see: Lessons beside the one editor. A lesson loads a deck and the reader presses Run in place.
options.cost: About 100 lines of page markup copied, plus a test that keeps both copies equal. Easy to undo.

options.label: B. Lessons on the front page
options.see: No copied markup. Eleven lessons wrap around the compiler on the first page.
options.cost: Goes against your request for a separate page. Buries the compiler. Moving out later means a rewrite.

options.label: C. Text page with share links
options.see: Each example is a link that opens the front page with that deck loaded.
options.cost: Cheapest. The reader flips between two pages and loses edit, run, compare on one screen.

scenes.say: Option A is a separate page with the same editor and script. Option B puts the lessons on the front page. Option C is a text page whose examples link back to the front page.

scenes.heading: A separate question: how much to teach
bullets: One guided walk through the 1962 sample: each lesson ties to existing tests.
A course of many small programs teaches more of the language.
But each program needs its own tapes built in, and its own test.
The course costs several times the walk to write and keep working.
scenes.say: Scope is a separate choice. A course of many small programs teaches more. But each one needs its own input tapes and its own test, or it breaks silently when the compiler changes.

scenes.heading: Recommendation
scenes.label: A, as one walk through the 1962 sample
reasons: Only form with the lesson and a running program on one screen, with one editor.
Its one cost, a copied block of markup, is caught by a cheap test.
Unedited-sample lessons reuse the existing tests; the edit lesson gets one of its own.
scenes.say: Take option A, scoped to one walk through the sample. It is the only form that keeps lesson and running program on one screen, with one editor. A cheap test guards its one cost.
